45|## Agent operating contract
46|
47|### Scope and execution
48|- Identify the requested outcome, affected components, and evidence needed
49|  to show completion before editing.
50|- Maintain one shared task with clear file ownership when delegating.
51|  Subagents inherit the same scope and permission limits.
52|- Complete authorized work autonomously. Do not ask permission for routine
53|  reads, isolated tests, reversible edits, or implementation choices.
54|- Follow demonstrated dependencies. Do not expand a repair into unrelated
55|  refactoring, new infrastructure, or speculative optimization.
56|- When new evidence expands the scope, state why and update the task.
57|
58|### Identity, permissions, and grants
59|- Use the identity and supported control-plane entry point assigned to
60|  the task. Preserve caller identity through delegated work.
61|- Existing authorization persists; do not ask for the same approval twice.
62|- A denied operation is evidence of a permission boundary. Record the
63|  operation, caller, exact missing capability or policy, and error.
64|- Do not bypass a denial through another identity, direct database edits,
65|  alternate transports, or privileged host commands.
66|- Do not broaden grants, weaken autonomy/security policies, expose secrets,
67|  or change unrelated identities to make a task pass.
68|- If a permission change is necessary, first prepare the smallest concrete
69|  change: affected principal, capability, resource scope, duration, expected
70|  effect, verification, and rollback. Request approval only for the part
71|  not already explicitly authorized.
72|
73|### Evidence and verification
74|- Distinguish proposed, implemented, tested, and deployed work.
75|- Verify the complete affected workflow, including failure and cancellation
76|  paths where relevant. A successful component test is not end-to-end proof.
77|- Use disposable fixtures and bounded workloads. Preserve authoritative
78|  data and unrelated work.
79|- Report failed or unavailable checks honestly. Do not convert missing
80|  coverage into a pass or repeatedly run unchanged failing checks.
81|- Prefer the smallest evidence-backed fix. Add technology only when a
82|  measured problem justifies its complexity.

85|- Sync decisions, conversations, and tool results to the shared repository
86|  with agent identity, timestamps, task ID, and source references.
87|- Use NotebookLM to recover context. Verify current code, permissions,
88|  configuration, and deployment state against their authoritative sources.
89|- Record the current commit, modified files, validation results, unresolved
90|  blockers, and exact next action. Update stale conclusions explicitly.
91|- Never describe planned work or another agent's claim as completed work.
92|
93|### Completion
94|- Finish with the outcome, changes, verification, remaining limitations,
95|  and deployment status.
96|- Stop when the requested outcome is verified; do not continue into
97|  speculative optimization or unrelated cleanup.

116|## Host-service policy (runit)
117|
118|This server runs **Artix Linux with glibc**, not Chimera or a musl-based host.
119|Build and test the server for `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu`. An installed musl
120|cross target or the Codex executable's own musl packaging does not change the
121|repository's native target. Any separate container portability test must name
122|its target and must not substitute for the Artix/glibc verification gate.
123|

126|- `/etc/runit/sv/<service>/run` is the service definition.
127|- Enabled by a symlink in `/etc/runit/runsvdir/default`.
128|- Update path: edit the `run` script or install a new binary, then `sudo sv restart <service>`.

Do not invoke `runsv`/`runsvdir` by hand. **s6 is legacy**: `service6`, `s6-rc`, `s6-*`, `/run/service` are stale — treat any doc assuming them as historical. Note: `/usr/local/bin/systemctl` on this host is a shim that returns plausible answers — using it masks the deprecation; always use `sv`. Do not use `systemctl` or other foreign service-manager CLIs. Container/app deployment uses D-Bus via `busctl`.

138|## Deployment (btrfs send/receive)
139|
140|**Owner clarification (2026-09-13): there is no deployment script. Deployment
141|is btrfs send/receive of the prepared filesystem snapshot.** The release
142|boundary is the snapshot's contents and the send/receive transfer. Existing
143|`deploy/` scripts are source/history or preparation tooling; neither
144|`build-golden.sh` nor `btrfs-layout.sh` defines the current deployment mechanism.
145|Never hand-copy binaries onto a running host as a deploy step.
146|
147|**Owner decision (2026-10-14): `./activate-golden.sh` at the repo root is the one
148|command for deploying a new version.** It runs the internal
149|`deploy/lib/golden/build-golden.sh` helper, then `op-release-launch release`:
150|btrfs send/receive of a golden snapshot into the inactive of two slots, then a
151|live read-only overlay swap at `/opt/op-dbus/current` (active + previous only;
152|`op-release-launch rollback` undoes it). The 2026-09-13 "no deployment script"
153|rule above is superseded for this entry point; the transport is still send/receive.
154|
155|`deploy/lib/golden/build-golden.sh` only populates and validates
156|`/opt/op-dbus/golden` from already built artifacts and an already sealed,
157|persisted catalog. Set `OP_PERSISTED_CATALOG_SOURCE` to use an isolated release
158|catalog; the script validates and copies it but never reseals it. It does not
159|create the read-only release snapshot, send
160|or receive it, activate a received filesystem, install files into the running
161|host, or restart services. `--golden-only` remains a compatibility alias for
162|its default behavior; the former `--live-only` and `--no-restart` modes are
163|retired. Snapshot creation, `btrfs send/receive`, target activation, and any
164|deliberate target service action are separate operator steps.
165|
166|```sh
167|CXXFLAGS="-include cstdint" cargo build --workspace --release
168|sudo target/release/opblob seal-shm            # explicitly reseal after the build
169|sudo target/release/opblob persist             # retain the catalog across reboot
170|```
171|
172|After builds, explicitly run the freshly built `opblob` to seal the release catalog; bridge startup only consumes sealed blobs and never reseals. For isolated release preparation, use `seal-plugins <new-catalog-dir>` and pass that catalog as `OP_PERSISTED_CATALOG_SOURCE`; publishing live SHM remains part of activation. Match the service's schema-shaping environment. The renamed cognitive code reads `COGNITIVE_*`: `COGNITIVE_QDRANT_URL` defaults to `http://127.0.0.1:6334`, matching the current `deploy/runit/op-grpc-bridge/run`; the historical `COGNITIVE_MCP_QDRANT_URL=http://10.200.0.2:6334` instruction is obsolete. After an explicit GNU-target build, use `target/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/release/opblob`, not an older default-target artifact. Verify the live and persisted catalogs match after activation. Review catalog removals and keep a recoverable copy before a full reseal, which sweeps plugin IDs absent from the build.
173|
174|The commands above describe build/catalog preparation, not deployment. Do not
175|infer a live install or restart from a successful build or snapshot preparation.

191|binary. Binary targets live in members: for example `op-grpc-bridge` and

Pre-existing scripts under `scripts/` (`export-llm-sessions-to-notebooklm-sources.py`, `or-fusion-archive.py`, `notebook-sources-cleanup.py`, etc.) are grandfathered — maintain them in place, don't propagate the pattern.

299|## Architecture — the load-bearing invariants (read these before touching plugins, state, or identity)
300|
301|- **Identity storage lifecycle (owner correction 2026-10-05).** Cozo owns identity-to-leaf/loop assignment and isolation. One immutable physical seed is shared through read-only views; each identity keeps its own writable leaf and the existing seven subvolumes. Only the external host provisioner may add a new blank leaf once, during explicit creation. Login, start, stop, logout, restart, bridge recovery and failed-start cleanup must NEVER add/remove Btrfs members. Start verifies/remounts the existing pair through the host mount owner; stop leaves membership and data intact. The bridge only verifies externally mounted storage and records logical attachment. Do not interpret `attached=false` as device removal. No root copies, snapshots, new subvolumes or OverlayFS fallback during identity provisioning. Never modify a seed while retained leaves depend on it. Older add-on-start/remove-on-stop guidance in source, handoffs and signals is superseded; do not restore it. Host release snapshot/send/receive below is a separate deployment mechanism.
302|- **D-Bus is the only control plane.** Every plugin is a D-Bus object at `/org/opdbus/v1/plugins/<name>` under `org.opdbus.v1`. No `Command::new(...)` subprocesses, no direct file reads for live state, no polling loops in plugin/service code. New backend capabilities register as plugins in `crates/op-plugins/src/default_registry.rs` — never as new gRPC proto service packages.
303|- **The plugin IS the schema — one source of truth, nonnegotiable.** That single schema is sealed into the blob, which IS the plugin. D-Bus method signatures, MCP tool inputs, gRPC shapes, and UI field renderers derive from it. Validate inputs against it. Each plugin defines its schema under `crates/op-plugins/src/state_plugins/`, using `plugin_scaffold_helpers.rs`. **There must be no parallel plugin schema source in a repository-level or plugin `schemas/` directory.** The former plugin capture directories, separate section files, and JSON-file loader have been removed. `crates/op-grpc-bridge/src/schema_loader.rs` still exists by name, but it reads only a manifest-pinned `PluginSchema` from the sealed blob catalog; it is not a file-schema fallback. **Owner correction (2026-10-18): capture threetched's full `config schema` from the verified binary on every seal.** The shared capture fixes the runtime config directory, checks the binary and manifest, and supplies native_config, MCP, model_routes, plugins and skill_bundles. `tched_router_contract.rs` contains only access/section helpers; the embedded UPSTREAM IMPORT is retired. Build-time generated bridge contracts explicitly prepare the same capture; runtime consumes the sealed catalog and never starts capture as a fallback. Do not restore an embedded schema or add independent captures using the sealer's ambient environment. The per-section generator and generated surface were retired on 2026-10-04. Older docs claiming a single `plugin_schema_defs.rs` are also stale — that file does not exist.
304|- **The sealed blob IS the plugin.** Present state lives in the sealed blob catalog at `/dev/shm/opdbus/plugin-blobs/<plugin_id>.<schema_hash16>.blob`. A plugin exists ⟺ its blob is in the catalog. The sole writer is the blob sealer in `op-blob`. Consumers read SHM directly (zero-copy) — they never re-hash and never consult the Rust registry for existence. The old `/dev/shm/opdbus/schemas` folder and `live-schema.json` are gone.
305|- **MutationEngine owns state; streaming comes from SHM (owner reaffirmed 2026-09-13).** MutationEngine folds authoritative backend results into the complete state tree, including child objects, and commits that state to canonical SHM before change notifications. Child updates/deletions must preserve unrelated children and parent fields. Existing subscriptions derive their values from committed SHM; an in-memory event payload, method argument, or generator buffer is not a second state authority. Preserve verified principal/session scope for private state. Do not add a separate per-method streaming control plane or claim a buffered unary response provides state streaming.
306|- **MCP gateway (settled).** One public MCP door: `:8090` on `op-grpc-bridge` (cognitive MCP is in-process there; no standalone `op-cognitive-mcp` runit service). `compact_mcp` is a retired plugin id. Compact *mode* (4 meta-tools) is in-process in op-web for the singleton control-plane chatbot; it is not an MCP plugin and not a second listener. Never create new shims or point external clients at `op-assistant-grpc`.
307|- **External binaries back plugins; the plugin remains the single schema source.** 3tched-router / tched-router (`tched_router` in code) is the framework/schema/plugin integration backed by the autonomous `/usr/bin/threetched` executable. The reproducible threetched input is pinned in `vendor/tched-router/source.pin`; `vendor/tched-router/build-threetched.sh` applies the checked-in patches and emits `target/threetched-artifacts/tched-router/{threetched,manifest.json}` without installing it. `build-golden.sh` validates the pin, patch and binary provenance, then stages the binary, `/usr/share/op-dbus/threetched-manifests/tched-router.json`, `/etc/op-dbus/threetched-runtime.toml`, and the tracked default skill bundle into the golden filesystem. The `tched-router` runit service verifies that manifest, exact commit, binary digest, and version before exec, then seeds its private runtime config and skills from those staged bootstrap files. A fresh checkout includes the digest-pinned upstream source archive, patches and build recipe; the helper verifies and uses that archive by default. Cargo registry dependencies and system build tools still need provisioning. Owner correction (2026-10-11): the executable and runtime-facing branding are lowercase `threetched`; the FUSE discovery source is `threetched-surface.rs`. Preserve upstream repository URLs, licenses and historical provenance. The former instruction to keep the executable named zeroclaw is superseded. The plugin contract remains `tched_router_contract.rs`, and source attribution may identify `zeroclaw config schema`.
308|- **Owner-confirmed lifecycle and model roles (2026-09-13, reaffirmed 2026-09-14).** Waypipe is retired: its crate directory, Cargo membership, binary target and protocol are absent; `retired-binaries`/`retired-services` prevent stale build or service artifacts from entering golden. {'content': '1|---\n2|name: btrfs\n3|description: >\n4|  Btrfs filesystem administration: subvolumes, snapshots, rollback, balance,\n5|  scrub, RAID profiles, compression, quotas, send/receive backups, and\n6|  troubleshooting.\n7|  MUST consult when installing, configuring, or troubleshooting btrfs.\n8|triggerPhrases:\n9|  - "btrfs"\n10|  - "Btrfs"\n11|  - "btrfs snapshot"\n12|  - "btrfs subvolume"\n13|  - "btrfs balance"\n14|  - "btrfs scrub"\n15|  - "copy-on-write filesystem"\n16|  - "CoW filesystem"\n17|  - "btrfs-progs"\n18|  - "mkfs.btrfs"\n19|  - "snapper"\n20|  - "btrbk"\n21|globs:\n22|  - "**/fstab"\n23|  - "**/etc/fstab"\n24|last_verified: "unverified"\n25|---\n26|\n27|## Identity\n28|\n29|| Property | Value |\n30||----------|-------|\n31|| **Type** | Kernel built-in filesystem (no loadable module needed on most distros) |\n32|| **CLI tool** | `btrfs` (subcommands: `filesystem`, `subvolume`, `balance`, `scrub`, `device`, `quota`, `qgroup`, `check`, `defragment`, `rescue`) |\n33|| **Distro install** | `apt install btrfs-progs` / `dnf install btrfs-progs` |\n34|| **Create** | `mkfs.btrfs` |\n35|| **Kernel version matters** | Significant stability improvements landed between 4.x and 6.x; older kernels have known bugs with RAID-5/6 and balance |\n36|\n37|## Quick Start\n38|\n39|```bash\n40|sudo apt install btrfs-progs\n41|sudo mkfs.btrfs -L mydata /dev/sdX1\n42|sudo mount /dev/sdX1 /mnt/mydata\n43|btrfs filesystem show /mnt/mydata\n44|btrfs device stats /mnt/mydata\n45|```\n46|\n47|## Key Operations\n48|\n49|| Task | Command |\n50||------|---------|\n51|| Show filesystems | `btrfs filesystem show` |\n52|| Filesystem usage (detailed) | `btrfs filesystem usage /mount` |\n53|| List subvolumes | `btrfs subvolume list /mount` |\n54|| Create subvolume | `btrfs subvolume create /mount/name` |\n55|| Delete subvolume | `btrfs subvolume delete /mount/name` |\n56|| Create read-write snapshot | `btrfs subvolume snapshot /mount/src /mount/dst` |\n57|| Create read-only snapshot | `btrfs subvolume snapshot -r /mount/src /mount/dst` |\n58|| Rollback: delete current, rename snapshot | `btrfs subvolume delete /mount/@; mv /mount/@snapshot /mount/@` |\n59|| Rollback: recreate subvolume from snapshot | `btrfs subvolume snapshot /mount/@snapshot /mount/@` |\n60|| Balance start (all chunks) | `btrfs balance start /mount` |\n61|| Balance start (metadata only) | `btrfs balance start -mconvert=raid1 /mount` |\n62|| Balance status | `btrfs balance status /mount` |\n63|| Balance cancel | `btrfs balance cancel /mount` |\n64|| Scrub start | `btrfs scrub start /mount` |\n65|| Scrub status | `btrfs scrub status /mount` |\n66|| Scrub cancel | `btrfs scrub cancel /mount` |\n67|| Check filesystem (read-only) | `btrfs check /dev/sdX` (unmounted) |\n68|| Defragment file or directory | `btrfs filesystem defragment -r /mount` |\n69|| Resize (grow) | `btrfs filesystem resize max /mount` |\n70|| Resize (shrink) | `btrfs filesystem resize -10G /mount` |\n71|| Add device | `btrfs device add /dev/sdY /mount` |\n72|| Remove device | `btrfs device remove /dev/sdY /mount` |\n73|| Device read/write error stats | `btrfs device stats /mount` |\n74|| Enable quotas | `btrfs quota enable /mount` |\n75|| Show qgroup usage | `btrfs qgroup show -reF /mount` |\n76|\n77|## Expected State\n78|\n79|- `btrfs device stats /mount` → all counters are `0` (any non-zero value is a read/write error)\n80|- `btrfs scrub status /mount` → `Status: finished` with `0 errors`\n81|- `btrfs balance status /mount` → `No balance found on \'/mount\'` when idle\n82|- `btrfs filesystem usage /mount` → Data and metadata ratios show reasonable allocation (metadata should not be >80% full)\n83|\n84|## Health Checks\n85|\n86|1. `btrfs device stats /mount` → all counters `0`; any non-zero value means hardware errors, act immediately\n87|2. `btrfs filesystem usage /mount` → check both Data and Metadata sections; metadata ENOSPC is the most common silent failure\n88|3. `btrfs scrub status /mount` → verify last scrub completed with no errors; schedule scrubs monthly via systemd timer or cron\n89|4. `btrfs subvolume list /mount` → audit snapshot count; accumulation fills disk without appearing in normal `df` output\n90|\n91|## Common Failures\n92|\n93|| Symptom | Cause | Fix |\n94||---------|-------|-----|\n95|| `no space left on device` but `df` shows free space | Metadata chunks exhausted while data chunks exist | `btrfs filesystem usage /mount` — run `btrfs balance start -dusage=50 /mount` to rebalance underused chunks |\n96|| RAID-1 on data but single on metadata | Dangerous default when adding a second disk; metadata is not redundant | `btrfs filesystem usage /mount` — check metadata profile; run `btrfs balance start -mconvert=raid1 /mount` |\n97|| Filesystem mounts read-only | Encountered an error it cannot self-correct | Check `dmesg | grep -i btrfs`; run `btrfs check /dev/sdX` on unmounted device to assess damage |\n98|| Balance fails with ENOSPC mid-run | Not enough free space to relocate all chunks | Use `-dusage=<N>` filter to relocate only partially-used chunks first; free up space before retrying |\n99|| Qgroup show reports inflated usage | Qgroups track snapshot references — shared data counted in each | Shared data is expected; use `btrfs qgroup show -reF` to see exclusive vs shared bytes |\n100|| Snapshot accumulation fills disk | Old snapshots reference deleted data, preventing space reclaim | `btrfs subvolume list /mount | grep snapshot` — delete old snapshots with `btrfs subvolume delete` |\n101|| `btrfs check --repair` made it worse | `--repair` is not safe for general use and can corrupt data | Never run `--repair` without consulting upstream; use `rescue` subcommands instead |\n102|| Filesystem errors after kernel upgrade | Older on-disk format or regression | Check `dmesg`; downgrade kernel or use `btrfs rescue` tools; check known issues for your kernel version |\n103|\n104|## Pain Points\n105|\n106|- **ENOSPC due to metadata/data imbalance**: The most common Btrfs "gotcha". Btrfs allocates space in chunks — if metadata chunks fill up, writes fail even when data chunks are available and `df` still shows free space. Fix: `btrfs balance start -dusage=50 /mount` to reclaim partially-empty chunks. This is not a bug — it is the expected behavior when chunk allocation becomes imbalanced.\n107|- **Mixed RAID profiles between data and metadata**: Adding a second disk does not automatically mirror metadata. A system can have `RAID1` data but `single` metadata, meaning metadata loss on one disk is fatal. Always explicitly set both with `-d` and `-m` flags.\n108|- **Snapshots are instant but they accumulate**: Snapshot creation is O(1) and free. Deletion requires reference counting and can be slow. Unreferenced snapshots hold on to deleted data indefinitely — disk usage only decreases after snapshot deletion completes.\n109|- **`btrfs check` is slow and `--repair` is risky**: Unlike `fsck.ext4`, Btrfs check does not have a safe repair mode. `--repair` can corrupt a filesystem that `check` reports as damaged. Prefer `btrfs rescue` subcommands (`zero-log`, `fix-device-size`) for targeted fixes.\n110|- **Btrfs RAID-5/6 has known parity issues**: As of kernels through 6.x, Btrfs RAID-5 and RAID-6 have unresolved write-hole bugs. Do not use RAID-5/6 for data you care about. Use RAID-1 or RAID-10 instead.\n111|- **Send/receive for backups**: `btrfs send` / `btrfs receive` is efficient for incremental backups using read-only snapshots as base references. Tools like `snapper` and `btrbk` automate the snapshot lifecycle and send/receive workflow — prefer them over manual scripting.\n112|- **CoW fragmentation on databases and VMs**: Copy-on-write writes new data to new locations, which fragments sequential files over time. Use `nodatacow` mount option (or `chattr +C`) for VM disk images, database files, and other large randomly-written files. `nodatacow` also disables checksums for those files.\n113|\n114|## See Also\n115|\n116|- **ext4** — Traditional Linux filesystem without CoW overhead; use when you need maximum compatibility and don\'t need snapshots\n117|- **xfs** — High-performance filesystem for large sequential I/O; use for databases and media workloads where CoW fragmentation is a concern\n118|- **zfs** — Full storage stack with pooling and replication; use when you need enterprise-grade checksums and send/receive without kernel version sensitivity\n119|- **lvm** — Logical volume manager; provides snapshot and resize capabilities at the block layer beneath btrfs\n120|\n121|## References\n122|\n123|See `references/` for:\n124|- `btrfs-options.md` — mkfs and mount options organized by category\n125|- `common-patterns.md` — filesystem setup, subvolume layouts, snapshots, rollback, backup, RAID, and compression\n126|- `docs.md` — official documentation and community links', 'total_lines': 126, 'file_size': 8377, 'truncated': False, 'is_binary': False, 'is_image': False, 'not_found': False}

{'content': '1|---\n2|name: rust-memory-optimization\n3|description: |\n4|  Memory optimization and allocation reduction in Rust. Use when:\n5|  - User is designing memory-sensitive or low-latency systems\n6|  - Optimizing data structures to reduce memory footprint\n7|  - Replacing heap allocations with stack-allocated/bounded structures (SmallVec, ArrayVec, ThinVec)\n8|  - Handling small strings with optimizations (CompactString)\n9|  - Reusing collections via clear() in loops\n10|  - Implementing zero-copy decoding and references\n11|  - Structuring arena-allocated memory (Bumpalo)\n12|  - Measuring memory usage, profiling heap, or diagnosing leaks\n13|---\n14|\n15|\n16|\n17|## Quick Navigation\n18|\n19|- [references/stack_allocations.md](references/stack_allocations.md)\n20|- [references/arenas.md](references/arenas.md)\n21|\n22|# Rust Memory Optimization Guide\n23|\n24|Advanced strategies for reducing allocations, shrinking layout sizes, and boosting performance.\n25|\n26|## Core Rules & Patterns\n27|\n28|### 1. Bounded Heap-Free Collections\n29|For collections that are usually small, avoid standard vectors to bypass heap allocations.\n30|- **`SmallVec`**: Stack-allocated up to a threshold, overflows to the heap.\n31|- **`ArrayVec`**: Fixed-capacity array wrapper; never allocates on the heap.\n32|- **`ThinVec`**: Only takes a single pointer size when empty, reducing size in enum layouts.\n33|\n34|```rust\n35|use smallvec::{smallvec, SmallVec};\n36|use arrayvec::ArrayVec;\n37|\n38|// SmallVec: Allocates 4 items on the stack. Goes to heap only if count > 4.\n39|let mut local_tags: SmallVec<[String; 4]> = smallvec![];\n40|local_tags.push("Rust".to_string());\n41|\n42|// ArrayVec: Absolute limit of 8 items on the stack. No heap overflow.\n43|let mut coordinates: ArrayVec<f64, 8> = ArrayVec::new();\n44|coordinates.push(42.0);\n45|```\n46|\n47|### 2. Small String Optimization (SSO)\n48|Standard `String` consumes 24 bytes and allocates heap space immediately. Use `CompactString` for inline small strings (under 24 bytes) without allocating.\n49|\n50|```rust\n51|use compact_str::CompactString;\n52|\n53|// No heap allocation for strings <= 24 characters\n54|let username = CompactString::new("user_123");\n55|```\n56|\n57|### 3. Boxed Slices vs Vectors\n58|If a collection\'s size is determined once at initialization and never changes, convert it from `Vec<T>` to `Box<[T]>` to save 8 bytes of stack capacity space.\n59|\n60|```rust\n61|let items_vec: Vec<i32> = vec![1, 2, 3];\n62|\n63|// Save capacity field (shrinks stack representation from 24 to 16 bytes)\n64|let items_slice: Box<[i32]> = items_vec.into_boxed_slice();\n65|```\n66|\n67|### 4. Zero-Copy Patterns\n68|Instead of cloning or allocating strings, hold references to existing memory using slices or crates like `bytes::Bytes`.\n69|\n70|```rust\n71|use bytes::Bytes;\n72|\n73|pub struct Message {\n74|    // Zero-copy reference-counted byte buffer slice\n75|    pub payload: Bytes,\n76|}\n77|\n78|// Can be sliced and shared among threads without cloning underlying memory\n79|let original = Bytes::from(vec![0; 1024]);\n80|let slice = original.slice(0..100); \n81|```\n82|\n83|### 5. Arena Allocation\n84|For batch allocation where structures share a lifecycle (e.g. AST parsing), use arena allocators (`bumpalo`) to allocate items sequentially in a continuous region of memory and free them all at once.\n85|\n86|```rust\n87|use bumpalo::Bump;\n88|\n89|let bump = Bump::new();\n90|\n91|// Allocates quickly on the bump arena\n92|let string_ref = bump.alloc_str("dynamic string");\n93|let int_ref = bump.alloc(42);\n94|\n95|// Entire arena is cleared at once on drop\n96|```\n97|\n98|### 6. Collection Reuse\n99|Reuse collection allocations in performance-critical loops with `.clear()` instead of re-instantiating.\n100|\n101|```rust\n102|// Bad: Allocates a new vector every iteration\n103|for item in feed {\n104|    let mut batch = Vec::new();\n105|    batch.push(item);\n106|}\n107|\n108|// Good: Reuses allocation buffer\n109|let mut batch = Vec::with_capacity(100);\n110|for item in feed {\n111|    batch.clear();\n112|    batch.push(item);\n113|}\n114|```\n115|\n116|## Layout Awareness\n117|\n118|Use `std::mem::size_of` to understand data layout.\n119|\n120|```rust\n121|println!("User size: {}", std::mem::size_of::<User>());\n122|```\n123|\n124|Reorder fields to reduce padding only when the type is numerous or hot.\n125|\n126|```rust\n127|// Often smaller: group large-alignment fields first\n128|struct Record {\n129|    id: u64,\n130|    flags: u32,\n131|    kind: u8,\n132|}\n133|```\n134|\n135|## String Strategy\n136|\n137|```rust\n138|fn label<\'a>(name: &\'a str, fallback: &\'a str) -> std::borrow::Cow<\'a, str> {\n139|    if name.is_empty() { fallback.into() } else { name.into() }\n140|}\n141|```\n142|\n143|Avoid `format!` in tight loops. Reuse buffers with `clear()`.\n144|\n145|## Zero-Copy Parsing\n146|\n147|Return slices into the input when the input outlives parsed data.\n148|\n149|```rust\n150|pub struct Header<\'a> {\n151|    pub name: &\'a str,\n152|    pub value: &\'a str,\n153|}\n154|```\n155|\n156|Do not force zero-copy when it creates unmanageable lifetimes for little gain.\n157|\n158|## ThinVec for Enum Payloads\n159|\n160|When enums contain `Vec` variants, `ThinVec` reduces the enum size by storing only a pointer when empty:\n161|\n162|```rust\n163|use thin_vec::ThinVec;\n164|\n165|// Regular Vec in an enum makes the enum 24+ bytes even when empty\n166|enum Node {\n167|    Leaf(i64),\n168|    Children(Vec<Node>),     // 24 bytes for Vec\n169|}\n170|\n171|// ThinVec only stores 8 bytes (a pointer) when empty\n172|enum NodeOptimized {\n173|    Leaf(i64),\n174|    Children(ThinVec<Node>), // 8 bytes for ThinVec\n175|}\n176|```\n177|\n178|## Cow for Conditional Ownership\n179|\n180|```rust\n181|use std::borrow::Cow;\n182|\n183|pub struct Error {\n184|    message: Cow<\'static, str>,\n185|}\n186|\n187|impl Error {\n188|    // No allocation for static messages\n189|    pub fn new(msg: &\'static str) -> Self {\n190|        Self { message: Cow::Borrowed(msg) }\n191|    }\n192|\n193|    // Allocates only when dynamic\n194|    pub fn with_detail(msg: String) -> Self {\n195|        Self { message: Cow::Owned(msg) }\n196|    }\n197|}\n198|```\n199|\n200|## Arc vs Rc Trade-offs\n201|\n202|```rust\n203|use std::rc::Rc;\n204|use std::sync::Arc;\n205|\n206|// Single-threaded shared ownership — cheaper than Arc\n207|let shared = Rc::new(large_data);\n208|\n209|// Multi-threaded shared ownership — required across threads\n210|let shared = Arc::new(large_data);\n211|```\n212|\n213|Prefer `Rc` when data never crosses thread boundaries. `Arc` adds atomic reference counting overhead.\n214|\n215|## HashMap Memory Optimization\n216|\n217|```rust\n218|use hashbrown::HashMap;\n219|\n220|// hashbrown\'s HashMap uses less memory than std\'s and is faster\n221|let mut map: HashMap<String, i32> = HashMap::with_capacity(128);\n222|\n223|// Reserve capacity upfront to avoid rehashing\n224|map.reserve(expected_count);\n225|\n226|// Consider FxHashMap for non-adversarial keys\n227|use rustc_hash::FxHashMap;\n228|let mut fast_map: FxHashMap<String, i32> = FxHashMap::default();\n229|```\n230|\n231|## Stack vs Heap Decision Matrix\n232|\n233|| Type | Stack Size | Heap Alloc | Use When |\n234||------|-----------|------------|----------|\n235|| `String` | 24 bytes | Yes | Owns mutable text |\n236|| `&str` | 16 bytes | No | Borrowed text, lifetime bound |\n237|| `CompactString` | 24 # Systematic Debugging

## Overview

Random fixes waste time and create new bugs. Quick patches mask underlying issues.

**Core principle:** ALWAYS find root cause before attempting fixes. Symptom fixes are failure.

**Violating the letter of this process is violating the spirit of debugging.**

## The Iron Law

```
NO FIXES WITHOUT ROOT CAUSE INVESTIGATION FIRST
```

If you haven't completed Phase 1, you cannot propose fixes.

## The Feedback Loop Rule

The feedback loop is the debugging work. Before reading code to build a theory, create or identify a **tight** command that can go red on the user's exact symptom and green when the bug is fixed. A tight loop is fast, deterministic, agent-runnable, and specific enough to catch this bug — not merely "doesn't crash".

When a clean repro is hard, spend disproportionate effort building the loop. Guessing without a red-capable loop is the failure mode this skill exists to prevent.

## When to Use

Use for ANY technical issue:
- Test failures
- Bugs in production
- Unexpected behavior
- Performance problems
- Build failures
- Integration issues

**Use this ESPECIALLY when:**
- Under time pressure (emergencies make guessing tempting)
- "Just one quick fix" seems obvious
- You've already tried multiple fixes
- Previous fix didn't work
- You don't fully understand the issue

**Don't skip when:**
- Issue seems simple (simple bugs have root causes too)
- You're in a hurry (rushing guarantees rework)
- Someone wants it fixed NOW (systematic is faster than thrashing)

## The Four Phases

You MUST complete each phase before proceeding to the next.

---

## Phase 1: Root Cause Investigation

**BEFORE attempting ANY fix:**

### 1. Read Error Messages Carefully

- Don't skip past errors or warnings
- They often contain the exact solution
- Read stack traces completely
- Note line numbers, file paths, error codes

**Action:** Use `read_file` on the relevant source files. Use `search_files` to find the error string in the codebase.

### 2. Build a Tight Feedback Loop

- Can you trigger the user's exact symptom with one command?
- Does the command fail for this bug and only pass once the bug is fixed?
- Is it fast enough to run repeatedly?
- Is it deterministic? For flaky bugs, can you raise the reproduction rate high enough to debug?
- If not reproducible → gather more data, don't guess.

**Ways to construct a loop — try in roughly this order:**

1. **Failing test** at the seam that reaches the bug: unit, integration, or end-to-end.
2. **HTTP script / curl** against a running dev server.
3. **CLI invocation** with fixture input, diffing stdout/stderr against expected output.
4. **Headless browser script** (Playwright/Puppeteer) asserting on DOM, console, or network.
5. **Replay a captured trace**: HAR, request payload, event log, queue message, or webhook body.
6. **Throwaway harness** that boots the smallest useful slice of the system and calls the failing path.
7. **Property / fuzz loop** when the bug is intermittent wrong output over a broad input space.
8. **Bisection harness** suitable for `git bisect run` when the bug appeared between two known states.
9. **Differential loop** comparing old vs new version, two configs, two providers, or two datasets.
10. **Human-in-the-loop script** only as a last resort: script the human steps and capture their result so the loop stays structured.

**Tighten the loop once it exists:**

- Make it faster: cache setup, narrow scope, skip unrelated initialization.
- Make the signal sharper: assert the exact symptom, not generic success.
- Make it more deterministic: pin time, seed randomness, isolate filesystem, freeze network.

For non-deterministic bugs, the immediate goal is a higher reproduction rate, not perfection. Run the trigger 100x, parallelize, add stress, narrow timing windows, or inject sleeps. A 50% flake is debuggable; a 1% flake usually is not.

**Action:** Use the `terminal` tool to run the tight loop:

```bash
# Run a specific failing test
pytest tests/test_module.py::test_name -v

# Or run a scripted repro
python scripts/repro_bug.py

# Or run a high-repetition flaky repro
for i in {1..100}; do pytest tests/test_flake.py::test_name -q || break; done
```

### 3. Check Recent Changes

- What changed that could cause this?
- Git diff, recent commits
- New dependencies, config changes

**Action:**

```bash
# Recent commits
git log --oneline -10

# Uncommitted changes
git diff

# Changes in specific file
git log -p --follow src/problematic_file.py | head -100
```

### 4. Gather Evidence in Multi-Component Systems

**WHEN system has multiple components (API → service → database, CI → build → deploy):**

**BEFORE proposing fixes, add diagnostic instrumentation:**

For EACH component boundary:
- Log what data enters the component
- Log what data exits the component
- Verify environment/config propagation
- Check state at each layer

Run once to gather evidence showing WHERE it breaks.
THEN analyze evidence to identify the failing component.
THEN investigate that specific component.

### 5. Trace Data Flow

**WHEN error is deep in the call stack:**

- Where does the bad value originate?
- What called this function with the bad value?
- Keep tracing upstream until you find the source
- Fix at the source, not at the symptom

**Action:** Use `search_files` to trace references:

```python
# Find where the function is called
search_files("function_name(", path="src/", file_glob="*.py")

# Find where the variable is set
search_files("variable_name\\s*=", path="src/", file_glob="*.py")
```

### Phase 1 Completion Checklist

- [ ] Error messages fully read and understood
- [ ] A tight loop command exists and has been run at least once
- [ ] Loop is red-capable: it asserts the user's exact symptom, not a nearby failure
- [ ] Loop is deterministic, or a flaky bug has a high enough reproduction rate to debug
- [ ] Recent changes identified and reviewed
- [ ] Evidence gathered (logs, state, data flow)
- [ ] Problem isolated to specific component/code
- [ ] Root cause hypotheses can be stated and tested

**STOP:** Do not proceed to Phase 2 until you understand WHY it's happening.

---

## Phase 2: Pattern Analysis

**Find the pattern before fixing:**

### 0. Minimize the Reproduction

Once the loop is red, shrink the repro to the smallest scenario that still goes red. Cut inputs, callers, config, data, and steps **one at a time**, re-running the loop after each cut. Keep only what is load-bearing for the failure.

Done when removing any remaining element makes the loop go green. A minimal repro narrows the hypothesis space and often becomes the cleanest regression test.

### 1. Find Working Examples

- Locate similar working code in the same codebase
- What works that's similar to what's broken?

**Action:** Use `search_files` to find comparable patterns:

```python
search_files("similar_pattern", path="src/", file_glob="*.py")
```

### 2. Compare Against References

- If implementing a pattern, read the reference implementation COMPLETELY
- Don't skim — read every line
- Understand the pattern fully before applying

### 3. Identify Differences

- What's different between working and broken?
- List every difference, however small
- Don't assume "that can't matter"

### 4. Understand Dependencies

- What other components does this need?
- What settings, config, environment?
- What assumptions does it make?

---

## Phase 3: Hypothesis and Testing

**Scientific method:**

### 1. Form Ranked Falsifiable Hypotheses

- Generate 3–5 plausible hypotheses before testing any single one.
- Rank them by likelihood and cheapness to falsify.
- State the prediction each hypothesis makes: "If X is the cause, then changing or observing Y should make Z happen."
- Discard or sharpen any hypothesis that does not make a testable prediction.

If the user is present, show the ranked list before testing. They may have domain knowledge that instantly re-ranks it. If the user is AFK, proceed with your ranking.

### 2. Test Minimally

- Test the highest-ranked hypothesis with the smallest possible probe.
- Change one variable at a time.
- Don't fix multiple things at once.
- Prefer debugger/REPL inspection when available; one breakpoint beats ten logs.
- If you add logs, tag every temporary line with a unique prefix such as `[DEBUG-a4f2]` so cleanup is a single search.

### 3. Verify Before Continuing

- Did it work? → Phase 4
- Didn't work? → Form NEW hypothesis
- DON'T add more fixes on top

### 4. When You Don't Know

- Say "I don't understand X"
- Don't pretend to know
- Ask the user for help
- Research more

---

## Phase 4: Implementation

**Fix the root cause, not the symptom:**

### 1. Create Failing Test Case

- Simplest possible reproduction
- Automated test if possible
- MUST have before fixing
- Use the `test-driven-development` skill

### 2. Implement Single Fix

- Address the root cause identified
- ONE change at a time
- No "while I'm here" improvements
- No bundled refactoring

### 3. Verify Fix

```bash
# Run the specific regression test
pytest tests/test_module.py::test_regression -v

# Run full suite — no regressions
pytest tests/ -q
```

### 4. If Fix Doesn't Work — The Rule of Three

- **STOP.**
- Count: How many fixes have you tried?
- If < 3: Return to Phase 1, re-analyze with new information
- **If ≥ 3: STOP and question the architecture (step 5 below)**
- DON'T attempt Fix #4 without architectural discussion

### 5. If 3+ Fixes Failed: Question Architecture

**Pattern indicating an architectural problem:**
- Each fix reveals new shared state/coupling in a different place
- Fixes require "massive refactoring" to implement
- Each fix creates new symptoms elsewhere

**STOP and question fundamentals:**
- Is this pattern fundamentally sound?
- Are we "sticking with it through sheer inertia"?
- Should we refactor the architecture vs. continue fixing symptoms?

**Discuss with the user before attempting more fixes.**

This is NOT a failed hypothesis — this is a wrong architecture.

---

## Red Flags — STOP and Follow Process

If you catch yourself thinking:
- "Quick fix for now, investigate later"
- "Just try changing X and see if it works"
- "Add multiple changes, run tests"
- "Skip the test, I'll manually verify"
- "It's probably X, let me fix that"
- "I don't fully understand but this might work"
- "Pattern says X but I'll adapt it differently"
- "Here are the main problems: [lists fixes without investigation]"
- Proposing solutions before tracing data flow
- **"One more fix attempt" (when already tried 2+)**
- **Each fix reveals a new problem in a different place**

**ALL of these mean: STOP. Return to Phase 1.**

**If 3+ fixes failed:** Question the architecture (Phase 4 step 5).

## Common Rationalizations

| Excuse | Reality |
|--------|---------|
| "Issue is simple, don't need process" | Simple issues have root causes too. Process is fast for simple bugs. |
| "Emergency, no time for process" | Systematic debugging is FASTER than guess-and-check thrashing. |
| "Just try this first, then investigate" | First fix sets the pattern. Do it right from the start. |
| "I'll write test after confirming fix works" | Untested fixes don't stick. Test first proves it. |
| "Multiple fixes at once saves time" | Can't isolate what worked. Causes new bugs. |
| "Reference too long, I'll adapt the pattern" | Partial understanding guarantees bugs. Read it completely. |
| "I see the problem, let me fix it" | Seeing symptoms ≠ understanding root cause. |
| "One more fix attempt" (after 2+ failures) | 3+ failures = architectural problem. Question the pattern, don't fix again. |

## Quick Reference

| Phase | Key Activities | Success Criteria |
|-------|---------------|------------------|
| **1. Root Cause** | Read errors, reproduce, check changes, gather evidence, trace data flow | Understand WHAT and WHY |
| **2. Pattern** | Find working examples, compare, identify differences | Know what's different |
| **3. Hypothesis** | Form theory, test minimally, one variable at a time | Confirmed or new hypothesis |
| **4. Implementation** | Create regression test, fix root cause, verify | Bug resolved, all tests pass |

## Hermes Agent Integration

### Investigation Tools

Use these Hermes tools during Phase 1:

- **`search_files`** — Find error strings, trace function calls, locate patterns
- **`read_file`** — Read source code with line numbers for precise analysis
- **`terminal`** — Run tests, check git history, reproduce bugs
- **`web_search`/`web_extract`** — Research error messages, library docs

### With delegate_task

For complex multi-component debugging, dispatch investigation subagents:

```python
delegate_task(
    goal="Investigate why [specific test/behavior] fails",
    context="""
    Follow systematic-debugging skill:
    1. Read the error message carefully
    2. Reproduce the issue
    3. Trace the data flow to find root cause
    4. Report findings — do NOT fix yet

    Error: [paste full error]
    File: [path to failing code]
    Test command: [exact command]
    """,
    toolsets=['terminal', 'file']
)
```

### With test-driven-development

When fixing bugs:
1. Write a test that reproduces the bug (RED)
2. Debug systematically to find root cause
3. Fix the root cause (GREEN)
4. The test proves the fix and prevents regression

## Real-World Impact

From debugging sessions:
- Systematic approach: 15-30 minutes to fix
- Random fixes approach: 2-3 hours of thrashing
- First-time fix rate: 95% vs 40%
- New bugs introduced: Near zero vs common

**No shortcuts. No guessing. Systematic always wins.**

2|name: ovs-db-analysis
3|description: >-
4|  Analyze Open vSwitch data from sosreport — conf.db, OpenFlow dumps, port stats,
5|  tunnels, and datapath health. Use when troubleshooting OVS packet drops, flow
6|  performance, bridge/port/interface issues, DPDK vs kernel datapath, or when the
7|  user mentions sosreport openvswitch, ovs-ofctl, ovsdb-tool, or ovs-db-analysis.
8|---
9|
10|# OVS Database and Flow Analysis
11|
12|This skill provides detailed analysis of Open vSwitch (OVS) data collected via sosreport. It operates in four modes:
13|
14|1. **Default mode**: Full analysis - conf.db + all text files (requires ovsdb-tool, falls back to text files if not available)
15|2. **Database mode (`--db`)**: Database only - analyze conf.db (requires ovsdb-tool)
16|3. **Text files mode (`--flows-only`)**: Text files only - no ovsdb-tool needed
17|4. **Query mode (`--query`)**: Run custom OVSDB JSON queries (requires ovsdb-tool)
18|
19|## When to Use This Skill
20|
21|Use this skill when:
22|- **Troubleshooting packet drops** - Find drop flows being hit
23|- **Analyzing flow performance** - View top flows by packet count
24|- Analyzing OVS configuration from a sosreport
25|- Troubleshooting bridge, port, or interface issues
26|- Investigating DPDK vs kernelspace datapath
27|- Reviewing tunnel configurations (VXLAN, Geneve, GRE)
28|- Checking port statistics (drops, errors, traffic)
29|- Mapping Kubernetes pods to OVS interfaces
30|
31|## Prerequisites
32|
33|**Default mode** (full analysis):
34|- **ovsdb-tool** must be installed (from openvswitch package)
35|- Falls back to `--flows-only` if ovsdb-tool not found
36|- Sosreport with `sos_commands/openvswitch/` directory and `conf.db`
37|
38|**Database mode** (`--db`):
39|- **ovsdb-tool** must be installed (from openvswitch package)
40|  - Check: `which ovsdb-tool`
41|  - Fedora/RHEL: `sudo dnf install openvswitch`
42|  - Ubuntu/Debian: `sudo apt install openvswitch-common`
43|- Sosreport with `conf.db` file
44|
45|**Text files mode** (`--flows-only`):
46|- No special tools needed - works out of the box!
47|- Sosreport with `sos_commands/openvswitch/` directory
48|
49|**Query mode** (`--query`):
50|- **ovsdb-tool** must be installed
51|- Incompatible with `--flows-only`
52|
53|## File Locations in Sosreport
54|
55|The sosreport collects:
56|```
57|sosreport-hostname-date/
58|├── etc/openvswitch/conf.db              (OVS database - for --db mode)
59|├── var/lib/openvswitch/conf.db          (alternate location)
60|└── sos_commands/openvswitch/            (default mode uses these)
61|    ├── ovs-vsctl_-t_5_show              (topology)
62|    ├── ovs-vsctl_-t_5_list_bridge       (bridge details)
63|    ├── ovs-vsctl_-t_5_list_interface    (interface details)
64|    ├── ovs-vsctl_-t_5_list_Open_vSwitch (system info)
65|    ├── ovs-ofctl_dump-flows_<bridge>    (OpenFlow entries)
66|    ├── ovs-ofctl_dump-ports_<bridge>    (Port statistics)
67|    ├── ovs-appctl_coverage.show         (internal stats)
68|    ├── ovs-appctl_upcall.show           (datapath health)
69|    ├── ovs-appctl_tnl.ports.show_-v     (tunnel ports)
70|    └── ...
71|```
72|
73|## Analysis Script
74|
75|The analysis script is located at:
76|```
77|<plugin-root>/skills/ovs-db-analysis/scripts/analyze_ovs_db.py
78|```
79|
80|## Implementation Steps
81|
82|### Step 1: Locate the Analysis Script
83|
84|```bash
85|SCRIPT_PATH=$(find ~ -name "analyze_ovs_db.py" -path "*/sosreport/skills/ovs-db-analysis/scripts/*" 2>/dev/null | head -1)
86|
87|if [ -z "$SCRIPT_PATH" ]; then
88|    echo "ERROR: analyze_ovs_db.py script not found."
89|    exit 1
90|fi
91|```
92|
93|### Step 2: Run the Analysis
94|
95|```bash
96|# Default: Full analysis - conf.db + text files (requires ovsdb-tool)
97|python3 "$SCRIPT_PATH" /path/to/sosreport-hostname-date/
98|
99|# Analyze from archive
100|python3 "$SCRIPT_PATH" /path/to/sosreport-hostname-date.tar.xz
101|
102|# Database only mode (requires ovsdb-tool)
103|python3 "$SCRIPT_PATH" /path/to/sosreport/ --db
104|
105|# Text files only mode (no ovsdb-tool needed)
106|python3 "$SCRIPT_PATH" /path/to/sosreport/ --flows-only
107|```
108|
109|### Step 3: Custom Queries (Optional, requires --db)
110|
111|For specific investigations, use raw OVSDB queries:
112|
113|```bash
114|# Query all bridges
115|python3 "$SCRIPT_PATH" /path/to/sosreport/ --query '["Open_vSwitch", {"op":"select", "table":"Bridge", "where":[], "columns":["name","datapath_type","fail_mode"]}]'
116|
117|# Query VXLAN interfaces
118|python3 "$SCRIPT_PATH" /path/to/sosreport/ --query '["Open_vSwitch", {"op":"select", "table":"Interface", "where":[["type","==","vxlan"]], "columns":["name","options"]}]'
119|
120|# Query interfaces with errors
121|python3 "$SCRIPT_PATH" /path/to/sosreport/ --query '["Open_vSwitch", {"op":"select", "table":"Interface", "where":[], "columns":["name","error"]}]'
122|```
123|
124|## Analysis Output
125|
126|The default mode analyzes:
127|
128|| Analysis | Source File | Description |
129||----------|-------------|-------------|
130|| System Info | `ovs-vsctl_-t_5_list_Open_vSwitch` | OVS/DPDK version, system type, external IDs |
131|| Topology | `ovs-vsctl_-t_5_show` | Bridge overview with ports grouped by type |
132|| Bridge Details | `ovs-vsctl_-t_5_list_bridge` | Datapath type, fail mode, CT zones |
133|| Interfaces | `ovs-vsctl_-t_5_list_interface` | By type, pod interfaces with mapping |
134|| OpenFlow | `ovs-ofctl_dump-flows_*` | Flow counts, drops, top flows |
135|| Port Stats | `ovs-ofctl_dump-ports_*` | RX/TX drops and errors |
136|| Tunnels | `ovs-appctl_tnl.ports.show_-v` | Configured tunnel ports |
137|| Datapath Health | `ovs-appctl_upcall.show` | Flow table usage vs limit |
138|| OVS Stats | `ovs-appctl_coverage.show` | Internal counters (netlink, OVSDB, etc.) |
139|
140|## OpenFlow Analysis Features
141|
142|| Feature | Description |
143||---------|-------------|
144|| Flow Count | Total flows per bridge (total, drop, with hits) |
145|| Drop Detection | Flows with `actions=drop` that have packet hits |
146|| Top Flows | Most active flows sorted by n_packets |
147|| Table Distribution | Flow counts per OpenFlow table |
148|| Port Drops | RX/TX drop counters per port |
149|| Port Errors | RX/TX error counters per port |
150|| Datapath Health | Flow table usage vs limit (from upcall.show) |
151|| OVS Stats | Internal statistics (netlink, OpenFlow, OVSDB transactions) |
152|
153|## OVN Internal Tables (Ignore Drops in These)
154|
155|When analyzing drop flows in OVN-managed bridges (br-int), **ignore drops in table 44 and tables 64-87** as these are internal OVN mechanics, not security policy or real packet drops.
156|
157|> **⚠️ Note:** OVN and OVS are complex systems and table mappings can change between releases. Always verify drop analysis against the specific OVN version in use. When in doubt, check the OVN source code for your release.
158|
159|| Table | Name | Purpose |
160||-------|------|---------|
161|| **44** | **CHK_LB_OUTPUT** | **Loopback prevention - drops packets that would loop back (high volume, normal)** |
162|| 64 | SAVE_INPORT | Save ingress port for later |
163|| 65 | LOG_TO_PHY | Logical to physical mapping |
164|| 66 | MAC_BINDING | MAC binding lookups |
165|| 67 | MAC_LOOKUP | MAC address table lookups |
166|| 68-69 | CHK_LB_HAIRPIN | Load balancer hairpin checks |
167|| 70 | CT_SNAT_HAIRPIN | Conntrack SNAT hairpin |
168|| 71-72 | GET/LOOKUP_FDB | FDB (forwarding DB) lookups |
169|| 73-74 | CHK_IN_PORT_SEC | Ingress port security |
170|| 75 | CHK_OUT_PORT_SEC | Egress port security |
171|| 76-77 | ECMP_NH | ECMP next-hop handling |
172|| 78 | CHK_LB_AFFINITY | Load balancer affinity |
173|| **79** | **MAC_CACHE_USE** | **MAC cache miss (high volume, normal)** |
174|| 80 | CT_ZONE_LOOKUP | Conntrack zone lookup |
175|| 81-83 | CT_ORIG_*_LOAD | Conntrack original tuple loading |
176|| 84 | FLOOD_REMOTE_CHASSIS | Remote chassis flooding |
177|| 85 | CT_STATE_SAVE | Conntrack state save |
178|| 86 | CT_ORIG_PROTO_LOAD | Conntrack protocol loading |
179|| 87 | GET_REMOTE_FDB | Remote FDB lookup |
180|
181|**Relevant drop tables for troubleshooting:**
182|- **Table 9**: Ingress ACLs - actual policy drops (look for `reg0=0x8000`)
183|- **Table 0**: Initial classification drops
184|- **Tables < 64**: Generally meaningful drops
185|
186|## Common Analysis Scenarios
187|
188|### 1. Troubleshooting Packet Drops
189|
190|```bash
191|# Quick analysis (default mode, no ovsdb-tool)
192|python3 "$SCRIPT_PATH" /path/to/sosreport/
193|```
194|
195|Look for:
196|- **ACTIVE DROP FLOWS** section showing flows dropping packets
197|- **PORT STATISTICS** showing ports with drops/errors
198|
199|### 2. Checking DPDK Configuration
200|
201|```bash
202|# Default mode shows DPDK info from text files
203|python3 "$SCRIPT_PATH" /path/to/sosreport/
204|
205|# Or use database mode for custom queries
206|python3 "$SCRIPT_PATH" /path/to/sosreport/ --query '["Open_vSwitch", {"op":"select", "table":"Open_vSwitch", "where":[], "columns":["dpdk_initialized","other_config"]}]'
207|```
208|
209|### 3. Investigating Pod Connectivity
210|
211|The interface analysis shows pod-to-OVS mapping:
212|- Interfaces with `external_ids` containing `iface-id`
213|- Interface names ending with `_h` (veth host side)
214|
215|### 4. Datapath Health Check
216|
217|The upcall stats show:
218|```
219|DATAPATH FLOW TABLE HEALTH
220|  Current flows: 155 / 200,000 (0.1% used)
221|  Average: 156, Max seen: 215
222|  ✓ Flow table healthy
223|```
224|
225|If usage > 90%, flows are being evicted too aggressively.

7|  writeback cache 一致性问题、多线程 FUSE daemon 死锁、容器中 /dev/fuse 权限问题、
8|  FUSE 性能退化等关键词时，必须使用本技能。
9|  覆盖场景：FUSE daemon 崩溃后 EIO、请求队列阻塞与 D 状态、max_read/max_write 配置不当、
10|  writeback cache 一致性问题、多线程 daemon 死锁、/dev/fuse 权限问题、内核 FUSE 模块 Bug、
11|  混合复杂 FUSE 故障。即使只收到"文件系统挂了"、"目录打不开"、"ls 卡死"但挂载点
12|  为 FUSE 类型时也应触发本技能。
13|  支持 FUSE 全链路诊断（sysfs 队列 → 内核参数 → daemon 进程 → 代码级根因）。

55|│                   三层下钻分析模型                                 │

64|│                                                                 │
65|│   L3: 代码/内核层    FUSE daemon 源码分析                       │
66|│                      内核 FUSE 模块参数 (/sys/module/fuse/)     │

68|│                      └─ 根因定位：daemon 崩溃 / 队列阻塞 / 配置  │

70|│   每层输出：证据 + 结论。L3 输出最终根因。                       │

105|## 第三节：诊断流程
106|
107|### L1: 系统层 — 基线采集与挂载点检查
108|
109|检查系统 FUSE 基础配置与挂载状态，判断是否为系统级配置问题。
110|
111|```bash
112|# 1. 检查 FUSE 挂载点
113|mount -t fuse
114|
115|# 2. 检查 /proc/mounts 中 FUSE 条目
116|grep fuse /proc/mounts
117|
118|# 3. 检查 FUSE 内核连接状态
119|ls /sys/fs/fuse/connections/ 2>/dev/null
120|
121|# 4. 检查 FUSE daemon 进程
122|ps aux | grep -E "[f]use|[F]ILESYSTEM_NAME"
123|
124|# 5. 基本连通性测试
125|ls -la <FUSE_mount_point>
126|stat <FUSE_mount_point>/test_file 2>&1
127|```
128|
129|**L1 结论判定**：
130|
131|| 现象 | 可能原因 | 下一层 |
132||------|---------|--------|
133|| 挂载点 ls 返回 EIO | FUSE daemon 崩溃 | Branch A |
134|| ls 卡死/D 状态 | 请求队列阻塞 | Branch B |
135|| 性能异常慢 | max_read/max_write 配置不当 | Branch C |
136|| 数据不一致 | writeback cache 问题 | Branch D |
137|| daemon 进程存在但无响应 | 多线程死锁 | Branch E |
138|| 权限 denied | /dev/fuse 权限 | Branch F |
139|| 内核 Panic/Oops | FUSE 内核模块 Bug | Branch G |
140|| 多种现象共存 | 混合故障 | Branch H |
141|
142|### L2 → L3: 类型层与代码根因层
143|
144|#### Branch A — FUSE Daemon 崩溃后 EIO
145|
146|**触发条件**：L1 中访问 FUSE 挂载点返回 "Transport endpoint is not connected" 或 EIO。
147|
148|```
149|L2 诊断：
150|├── 1. stat <mount_point>（确认 EIO 错误码）
151|├── 2. grep <mount_point> /proc/mounts（挂载条目是否仍存在）
152|├── 3. ls /sys/fs/fuse/connections/（连接是否已销毁）
153|├── 4. ps aux | grep <daemon_name>（daemon 进程是否存在）
154|├── 5. journalctl -u <daemon_service> --since "5 min ago"（daemon 退出日志）
155|├── 6. dmesg | grep -i fuse（内核 FUSE 消息）
156|├── 7. cat /sys/fs/fuse/connections/*/abort 2>/dev/null（abort 状态）
157|│
158|└── L3 根因判定：
159|    ├── daemon 进程不存在 + 连接已销毁 → daemon 崩溃/被 OOM Kill
160|    ├── daemon 进程不存在 + 连接残留 → daemon 退出但连接未清理
161|    ├── daemon 存在但连接状态异常 → daemon 内部状态机错误
162|    ├── dmesg 显示 "fuse: aborting connection" → 内核主动中止
163|    ├── OOM Killer 日志 → daemon 因内存超限被内核杀死
164|    └── 连接 abort 状态为 1 → 手动触发 abort 或 daemon 调用 abort
165|```
166|
167|**典型输出**：
168|```
169|结论: FUSE daemon 进程不存在（已崩溃），
170|      /sys/fs/fuse/connections/ 目录为空（连接已销毁）。
171|      dmesg 无 FUSE 相关错误，但 journalctl 显示 daemon 因
172|      SIGSEGV (signal 11) 退出。
173|根因: FUSE daemon 程序存在内存访问越界 Bug，导致段错误崩溃。
174|```
175|
176|#### Branch B — FUSE 请求队列阻塞
177|
178|**触发条件**：LS 卡死、进程 D 状态（uninterruptible sleep）、`/sys/fs/fuse/connections/*/waiting` 持续增长。
179|
180|```
181|L2 诊断：
182|├── 1. cat /sys/fs/fuse/connections/*/waiting（请求队列深度）
183|├── 2. cat /sys/fs/fuse/connections/*/max_background（最大后台请求数）
184|├── 3. ps aux | grep D | grep -v grep（D 状态进程列表）
185|├── 4. cat /proc/<D_pid>/stack（查看 D 状态内核栈）
186|├── 5. strace -e trace=write,read,ioctl -p <daemon_pid>（daemon 系统调用）
187|├── 6. cat /sys/fs/fuse/connections/*/congested_threshold_ms（拥塞阈值）
188|├── 7. dmesg | grep -i "fuse.*block"（阻塞告警）
189|│
190|└── L3 根因判定：
191|    ├── waiting 持续增长 + daemon 未处理请求 → daemon 侧线程阻塞
192|    ├── daemon 进程 strace 显示 read() 未被唤醒 → 内核/FUSE 调度问题
193|    ├── D 状态进程内核栈显示 fuse_request_send → 请求队列已满等待
194|    ├── max_background 设置过小 → 请求队列排队上限低导致积压
195|    ├── daemon write() 变慢或阻塞 → daemon 后端存储 I/O 瓶颈
196|    └── congested_threshold 触发 → FUSE 内核主动限流
197|```
198|
199|**典型输出**：
200|```
201|结论: /sys/fs/fuse/connections/*/waiting 持续增长（当前值: 512），
202|      进程 D 状态栈显示 fuse_request_send。
203|      strace 显示 daemon read() 调用未被及时唤醒。
204|根因: FUSE daemon 工作线程池太小或线程卡在后端 I/O 上，
205|      无法及时消费内核下发的 FUSE 请求。
206|```
207|
208|#### Branch C — max_read/max_write 配置不当
209|
210|**触发条件**：FUSE 文件系统性能显著低于预期，小文件/大文件读写性能异常。
211|
212|```
213|L2 诊断：
214|├── 1. cat /sys/fs/fuse/connections/*/max_read（当前 FUSE 最大读取大小）
215|├── 2. cat /sys/module/fuse/parameters/max_read（内核模块参数）
216|├── 3. mount | grep <fuse_type>（挂载参数 -o max_read=,max_write=）
217|├── 4. dd if=<mount_point>/test of=/dev/null bs=1M count=100（读性能测试）
218|├── 5. dd if=/dev/zero of=<mount_point>/test bs=1M count=100（写性能测试）
219|├── 6. iostat -x 1 <device>（底层 I/O 延迟）
220|├── 7. strace -e pread64,pwrite64 -p <daemon_pid>（系统调用大小对比）
221|│
222|└── L3 根因判定：
223|    ├── max_read=4096（4K）→ 每次读请求仅传输 4K，大文件读性能极差
224|    ├── max_write=4096（4K）→ 每次写请求仅传输 4K，写性能瓶颈
225|    ├── max_read 与底层存储块大小不匹配 → 产生大量小 I/O
226|    ├── 挂载时未指定 max_read= → 使用默认值（通常 1MB，但某些 FUSE 缩减）
227|    ├── daemon 未实现 readdir 缓存 → 目录遍历性能退化
228|    └── 内核 max_read 参数被 sysfs 限制 → 无法超过内核模块设置的上限
229|```
230|
231|**典型输出**：
232|```
233|结论: max_read=4096（4K），远低于默认 1MB。
234|      dd 读测试仅 12 MB/s，远低于预期 200+ MB/s。
235|      strace 确认每次 pread64 仅传输 4096 字节。
236|根因: FUSE 挂载时未指定 max_read，daemon 初始化协商值为 4K
237|      （libfuse 旧版本默认），导致大文件顺序读性能退化。
238|```
239|
240|#### Branch D — Writeback Cache 一致性问题
241|
242|**触发条件**：FUSE 文件系统写入后读取数据不一致、写入顺序错误、重复内容。
243|
244|```
245|L2 诊断：
246|├── 1. mount | grep <fuse_type> | grep -o "writeback_cache"（检查是否启用）
247|├── 2. cat /sys/module/fuse/parameters/use_writeback_cache（内核参数）
248|├── 3. echo "test" > <mount_point>/file && cat <mount_point>/file（一致性测试）
249|├── 4. strace -e write,pwrite64,fsync -p <daemon_pid>（跟踪写操作时序）
250|├── 5. dd if=/dev/urandom of=<mount_point>/test bs=4K count=100（并发写入）
251|├── 6. md5sum <mount_point>/test && sleep 1 && md5sum <mount_point>/test（变化检测）
252|├── 7. grep -i "fuse.*invalidate" /proc/<daemon_pid>/stack（缓存无效化状态）
253|│
254|└── L3 根因判定：
255|    ├── writeback_cache 启用但 daemon 未实现 ->release 回调 → 数据未刷入后端
256|    ├── 并发写入后的读取返回过期数据 → page cache 未正确无效化
257|    ├── daemon write() 返回成功但数据未持久化 → 缺少 fsync 语义
258|    ├── 内核 fuse_conn 中 writeback_cache=1 但后端不支持原子写
259|    ├── mmap 写入后数据丢失 → FUSE 不支持 shared mmap writeback cache
260|    └── multi-page writeback 顺序错误 → daemon 未按 LBA 顺序处理请求
261|```
262|
263|**典型输出**：
264|```
265|结论: writeback_cache 启用后，写入 100 个 4K 块后的 md5sum
266|      在不同读取时间点返回不同值。
267|      daemon 未实现 ->write() 回调的完整 writeback 语义。
268|根因: FUSE daemon 启用 writeback_cache 模式但未正确处理
269|      内核的 writeback 请求，page cache 与后端存储数据不一致。
270|```
271|
272|#### Branch E — 多线程 FUSE Daemon 死锁
273|
274|**触发条件**：FUSE daemon 进程存在但操作挂起，挂载点操作无响应。
275|
276|```
277|L2 诊断：
278|├── 1. ps -eLf | grep <daemon_name>（daemon 线程列表）
279|├── 2. cat /proc/<daemon_pid>/stack（主线程内核栈）
280|├── 3. for tid in $(ls /proc/<daemon_pid>/task/); do echo "TID:$tid"; cat /proc/$tid/stack 2>/dev/null; done
281|├── 4. strace -f -e trace=write,read,ioctl -p <daemon_pid>（多线程追踪）
282|├── 5. gdb -p <daemon_pid> -batch -ex "thread apply all bt"（全线程回溯）
283|├── 6. cat /sys/fs/fuse/connections/*/waiting（确认请求堆积）
284|├── 7. kill -USR1 <daemon_pid>（向 daemon 发送信号检查状态）
285|│
286|└── L3 根因判定：
287|    ├── 所有工作线程在 pthread_mutex_lock 等待 → 互斥锁死锁
288|    ├── 线程 A 持有锁 L1 等待锁 L2，线程 B 持有锁 L2 等待锁 L1 → 经典死锁
289|    ├── 工作线程在 write() 后端存储时阻塞 → I/O 死锁（等待自身填充）
290|    ├── 线程池所有线程都在 fuse_session_process 中 → 请求循环依赖
291|    ├── 主线程在 fuse_loop 中阻塞但工作线程已退出 → 线程管理 Bug
292|    └── daemon 中 fuse_reply_* 调用顺序错误 → 协议级死锁
293|```
294|
295|**典型输出**：
296|```
297|结论: daemon 4 个工作线程全部在 pthread_mutex_lock 等待。
298|      gdb 显示 Thread 1 持有 lock A 等待 lock B，
299|      Thread 2 持有 lock B 等待 lock A——经典 ABBA 死锁。
300|根因: FUSE daemon 中锁获取顺序不一致，导致多线程死锁，
301|      文件系统操作完全挂起。
302|```
303|
304|#### Branch F — /dev/fuse 设备权限问题
305|
306|**触发条件**：容器或非 root 用户启动 FUSE daemon 时出现 Permission denied。
307|
308|```
309|L2 诊断：
310|├── 1. ls -la /dev/fuse（设备节点权限）
311|├── 2. getfacl /dev/fuse（ACL 权限检查）
312|├── 3. cat /proc/<daemon_pid>/status | grep Cap（daemon 能力集）
313|├── 4. grep fuse /etc/group（fuse 用户组）
314|├── 5. groups <daemon_user>（用户所属组）
315|├── 6. cat /etc/fuse.conf（FUSE 全局配置）
316|├── 7. capsh --print | grep fuse（进程能力检查）
317|├── 8. container environment: cat /proc/1/cgroup（容器内 cgroup 检查）
318|│
319|└── L3 根因判定：
320|    ├── /dev/fuse 权限 0600 root:root → 非 root 用户无法访问
321|    ├── daemon 用户不在 fuse 组 → 缺少 /dev/fuse 访问权限
322|    ├── 容器内未挂载 /dev/fuse → 设备节点不存在
323|    ├── 容器缺少 CAP_SYS_ADMIN 或 CAP_MKNOD → 无法操作 FUSE 设备
324|    ├── user_allow_other 未在 /etc/fuse.conf 启用 → 无法使用 allow_other
325|    ├── AppArmor/SELinux 阻止 FUSE 操作 → 安全策略限制
326|    └── daemon 进程 capabilities 被移除 → container runtime 降权
327|```
328|
329|**典型输出**：
330|```
331|结论: /dev/fuse 权限 0600 root:root，daemon 以非 root 用户
332|      运行且不在 fuse 用户组中。
333|      daemon 启动日志显示 "Permission denied" 打开 /dev/fuse。
334|根因: /dev/fuse 设备节点仅 root 可读写，FUSE daemon
335|      以普通用户运行且未加入 fuse 组，无法打开设备。
336|```
337|
338|#### Branch G — FUSE 内核模块 Bug
339|
340|**触发条件**：内核 Panic、Oops、soft lockup 与 FUSE 相关，或已知 FUSE 内核 Bug。
341|
342|```
343|L2 诊断：
344|├── 1. dmesg | grep -iE "fuse|libfuse"（内核 FUSE 消息）
345|├── 2. dmesg | grep -iE "kernel panic|Oops|BUG|soft lockup"（内核异常）
346|├── 3. cat /sys/module/fuse/version（FUSE 模块版本）
347|├── 4. uname -r（内核版本）
348|├── 5. cat /proc/self/mounts | grep fuse（所有 FUSE 挂载）
349|├── 6. cat /sys/fs/fuse/connections/*/abort（abort 状态）
350|├── 7. test -f /var/crash/vmcore* 2>/dev/null && ls -lh /var/crash/（crash dump 检查）
351|├── 8. grep -i fuse /var/log/messages | tail -20（系统日志）
352|│
353|└── L3 根因判定：
354|    ├── 已知 FUSE 内核 Bug 列表匹配（CVE-xxxx-xxxx / 内核 commit）
355|    ├── 特定内核版本 + FUSE 版本组合已知不兼容
356|    ├── CR2 地址在 FUSE 模块区域内 → FUSE 内核模块导致 Panic
357|    ├── soft lockup 栈显示在 fuse_* 函数中 → FUSE 内核路径问题
358|    ├── 大规模并发操作触发的竞态条件 → 内核 FUSE 并发 Bug
359|    └── FUSE 模块参数不合理导致内核异常 → max_read 过小/过大
360|```
361|
362|**典型输出**：
363|```

3|# names are selectors, never identity authority. Preflight all boot selections
4|# before restoring anything; conflicting logical identities fail closed.

10|    path=$1
11|    [ "$(realpath -e -- "$path")" = "$path" ] || fail "noncanonical path: $path"
12|    while :; do
13|        [ ! -L "$path" ] && [ "$(stat -c %u -- "$path")" = 0 ] &&
14|            [ $((0$(stat -c %a -- "$path") & 022)) -eq 0 ] || fail "unsafe owner/mode: $path"
15|        [ "$path" != / ] || break
16|        path=$(dirname -- "$path")
17|    done
18|)
19|private_receipt() {
20|    secure_path "$1" || return 1
21|    [ -f "$1" ] && [ "$(stat -c %u:%g:%a "$1")" = 0:0:600 ]
22|}
23|wait_dep() {
24|    sv start "$1" >/dev/null 2>&1 || true
25|    i=0
26|    until sv check "$1" >/dev/null 2>&1; do
27|        i=$((i + 1))
28|        [ "$i" -ge 90 ] && fail "dependency $1 not ready after 90s"
29|        sleep 1
30|    done
31|}
32|wait_dep incus
33|i=0
34|until incus info >/dev/null 2>&1; do
35|    i=$((i + 1))
36|    [ "$i" -lt 60 ] || fail 'incusd API not ready'
37|    sleep 1
38|done
39|# Deliberate release-owned dependency selection; a partial/broken activated
40|# closure is an error, not permission to execute an older base helper.
41|if [ "${OP_IDENTITY_HELPER_DIR+x}" = x ]; then
42|    helper_dir=$OP_IDENTITY_HELPER_DIR
43|elif [ -e /usr/local/libexec/op-dbus/helpers ] || [ -L /usr/local/libexec/op-dbus/helpers ]; then
44|    helper_dir=/usr/local/libexec/op-dbus/helpers
45|else
46|    helper_dir=/usr/local/libexec/3tched
47|fi
48|helper_dir=$(realpath -e -- "$helper_dir") || fail 'selected helper directory absent'
49|secure_path "$helper_dir" || exit 1
50|for dependency in op-identity-root op-identity-image restore-chatbot-root runit-ready-signal; do
51|    secure_path "$helper_dir/$dependency" || exit 1
52|    [ -f "$helper_dir/$dependency" ] && [ -x "$helper_dir/$dependency" ] || fail "selected helper unavailable: $dependency"
53|done
54|helper=$helper_dir/op-identity-root
55|restore_helper=$helper_dir/restore-chatbot-root
56|# Keep the entire root-helper chain in the selected closure.
57|OP_IDENTITY_IMAGE_HELPER=$helper_dir/op-identity-image

59|chatbot_session=b0c777e3-0955-cd8b-3d01-ca12998cae28
60|physical=${OP_IDENTITY_SEED_STATE:-/var/lib/opdbus-runtime/seed-identities}

63|gpt_name=
64|physical_present=0

66|selected_sessions='|'
67|# GPT boot receipts attest completed adoption; restore --check verifies exact

69|# Never execute restoration while another receipt could name the same chatbot.
70|for receipt in /var/lib/3tched-leaf-pool/.provisioning/*.boot.json; do
71|    [ -e "$receipt" ] || [ -L "$receipt" ] || continue

80|for receipt in "$physical"/*/state.json; do

101|    [ "$expected" = "$actual" ] || fail "physical boot/storage pins differ: $name"
102|    session=$(jq -er .session "$receipt") || fail "missing physical session: $name"
103|    case "$selected_sessions" in
104|        *"|$session|"*) fail "conflicting boot receipts for logical identity $session; no roots restored" ;;
105|    esac
106|    selected_sessions="$selected_sessions$session|"
107|    physical_names="$physical_names $name"
108|done
109|failed=0
110|if [ -n "$gpt_name" ]; then
111|    "$restore_helper" "$gpt_name" || failed=$((failed + 1))
112|fi
113|seed_readonly_ready=0
114|for name in $physical_names; do
115|    receipt=$physical/$name/state.json
116|    marker=$physical/$name/boot-ready.json
117|    start_on_boot=$(jq -er '.start_on_boot|select(type=="boolean")|tostring' "$marker") || fail "invalid boot policy: $name"
118|    # The helper checks the complete boot/storage marker, native UUID and
119|    # session/key binding again under its lifecycle lock before touching roots.
120|    if [ "$seed_readonly_ready" -eq 0 ]; then
121|        "$helper" seed-readonly || fail 'physical seed read-only enforcement failed'
122|        seed_readonly_ready=1
123|    fi
124|    state=$(incus query "/1.0/instances/$name/state" | jq -er '.status') || state=unknown
125|    case "$state" in
126|        Running)
127|            if "$helper" seed-check "$name"; then
128|                "$helper" seed-lungs "$name" || failed=$((failed + 1))
129|            else failed=$((failed + 1)); fi
130|            ;;
131|        Stopped)
132|            if "$helper" seed-up "$name" && "$helper" seed-lungs "$name"; then
133|                if [ "$start_on_boot" = true ]; then incus start "$name" || failed=$((failed + 1))
134|                else echo "physical seed $name: storage restored; boot start disabled"; fi
135|            else failed=$((failed + 1)); fi
136|            ;;
137|        *) echo "physical seed $name: unsupported native status $state" >&2
138|            failed=$((failed + 1)) ;;
139|    esac
140|done
141|if [ "$physical_present" -eq 1 ] || [ "$gpt_present" -eq 1 ]; then
142|    # Never select legacy `up`: directly mounting the same seed conflicts with
143|    # retained sprouts even when another identity's root failed restoration.
144|    for image in "$legacy"/*/identity.img; do
145|        [ -f "$image" ] || continue
146|        name=$(basename "$(dirname "$image")")
147|        case "$selected_sessions" in
148|            *"|$name|"*) echo "legacy identity $name: suppressed by selected boot receipt"; continue ;;
149|        esac
150|        if [ "$name" = 3tchedChatbot ] && [ "$gpt_present" -eq 1 ]; then
151|            echo "legacy identity $name: suppressed by GPT boot receipt"
152|        elif [ -e "$physical/$name/state.json" ] || [ -L "$physical/$name/state.json" ]; then
153|            echo "legacy identity $name: suppressed by physical seed receipt"
154|        else
155|            echo "legacy identity $name: migration or independent lower required; shared seed direct mount suppressed" >&2
156|            failed=$((failed + 1))
157|        fi
158|    done
159|else
160|    "$helper" up || failed=$((failed + 1))
161|    "$helper" status || failed=$((failed + 1))
162|fi
163|[ "$failed" -eq 0 ] || fail "$failed identity root startup check(s) failed"
164|"$helper_dir/runit-ready-signal" identity-roots || exit 1

13|# --prepare-container defines the stopped chatbot and socket profile only;
14|# it does not bind the prepared root, adopt the identity or start the guest.
